tasks.registered_metrics_text:
a) Define the metric(s) to assess a property of an algorithm. These metrics should reflect the desired algorithm
properties described in assessment aim(s) (see above). State which metric(s) were used to compute the ranking(s) (if
any).
  • Example 1: Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC)
  • Example 2: Area under curve (AUC)
Two metrics will be used:
- Volumetric Dice
- Surface Dice


We have, from the annotation process used in KiTS21, collected three annotations for each region of interest for
the first 400 cases of our dataset. Based on these, we devised a strategy to dynamically determine a suitable
tolerance for each class on each case. We did this by finding the mean of the 95th percentile of the surface
distance of any two annotations of a single instance within each class. For KiTS23 we have decided to simply use



 2023 Kidney and Kidney Tumor Segmentation Challenge

the median of these KiTS21 tolerances for each class.


Where each metric is computed for each of the following evaluation classes:
- Union(Kidney, Tumor, Cyst)
- Union(Tumor, Cyst)
- Tumor


These metrics are determined per volume and then averaged.

b) Justify why the metric(s) was/were chosen, preferably with reference to the biomedical application.

Our two chosen metrics act together in complementary ways. Volumetric Dice does a nice job of capturing how
well the model allocated the 'bulk' of its predictions, whereas Surface Dice then measures how well the surface of
each ROI matches up with what was predicted, rightly penalizing cases in which small ROIs were missed entirely.


This combination of metrics was employed for KiTS21 and seemed to work quite well.
tasks.registered_ranking_text:
a) Describe the method used to compute a performance rank for all submitted algorithms based on the generated
metric results on the test cases. Typically the text will describe how results obtained per case and metric are aggregated
to arrive at a final score/ranking.

The final performance rank will be obtained by computing each metric's average across all regions across all cases,
and then performing a rank-then-aggregate operation by averaging each team's relative leaderboard position
between these two metrics. In cases where there is a tie, the Tumor Volumetric Dice will be used as a tiebreaker.

b) Describe the method(s) used to manage submissions with missing results on test cases.

Missing test case predictions will be assigned the lowest possible value (0.0) for each metric.

c) Justify why the described ranking scheme(s) was/were used.

The rank-then-aggregate paradigm is a simple and elegant way to use two metrics in combination without having
to worry too much about their relative scales such that one might unexpectedly dominate the other when
averaging them together, for example. Tumor Volumetric Dice is a suitable tiebreaker because Volumetric Dice
remains the most commonly-used segmentation metric, and Tumor is the most clinically-import region of interest
for this challenge.

registered_task_submissions.protocol_description: During the one week submission period, teams will request a 48 hour window at the beginning of which, an automated email will send them a link to download the test set images. They are required to then submit their predictions to CodaLab before the end of that 48 hour window. Otherwise they will be disqualified. The predictions will take the form of a zip archive of Nifti files of the same shape as the original images, with predicted segmentations represented in the form of integer values (1 for kidney, 2 for tumor, 3 for cyst). We understand the push for challenges to ask teams for containers, but after having tried this in 2021, a large number of participants experienced difficulty getting their containers to run within the allotted time and memory limit. We recognize that this is, in large part, our fault, since we apparently did not communicate these computational requirements to teams clearly enough or with enough emphasis. However, it speaks to the fact that teams would have modified their approaches had they known about the limitations, and computational efficiency is not what KiTS is meant to be about. KiTS aims to identify the best approach for automatic kidney tumor segmentation regardless of computational complexity. The concern that teams will cheat by intervening manually in their algorithm's predictions is nontrivial. However, by restricting teams to have the data for only 48 hours prior to their predictions being due, their time window for doing so is very limited. As the people annotating the data, we know very well that 48 hours is not nearly enough time to manually produce high-quality labels for our test set. As a further measure to prevent cheating in this way, after the leaderboard is published, each of the top 5 teams will be asked to produce a Docker container which faithfully reproduces the predictions that were submitted to the leaderboard. We plan to run submitted Docker containers on a P3.2xlarge EC2 instance with a single V100 GPU, and we will require that it takes no more than 2.5 hr per case. We feel that this hybrid approach strikes a balance between the administrative and infrastructure costs associated with algorithm submission and the risk of cheating associated with prediction submission. There is some risk that teams might share data between them within the submission window. In order to mitigate it, we will require that each team produce the following in order to receive a copy of the data: A complete manuscript, with the exception of final results A final list of contributors, including their ORCID A signed document in which they promise to abide by the terms of use which include a clause prohibiting data sharing It is our belief that it is unlikely for a team to go to all of the work to produce a manuscript, but then provide an unfair advantage to one of their competitors. Asking for author identifiers helps to ensure that the same team is not registering for multiple time windows under the guise of different teams. Finally, at the end of the day, some level of trust is still required (as is the case in evaluating virtually all research results). To this end, we will require teams to sign our terms of use and we will trust that they will not violate them. On top of all of this, we will also restrict the submission period to a single week, rather than two weeks as originally 2023 Kidney and Kidney Tumor Segmentation Challenge proposed. This will mitigate the impact of data sharing if it ultimately were to occur.
